profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the Slack platform team and the Developer Productivity team at a mid-size SaaS company. They are preparing a cross-team rollout of a new internal chatbot, 'Handbot', that posts release reminders, ownership nudges, and dependency summaries into engineering channels to reduce collaboration friction during feature delivery. The context is that the platform team has finished the event ingestion service, while the productivity team is wiring the bot into team workflows before a pilot with three backend squads next week. The agenda is to align on the integration interface, what the Friday handoff should contain, how the pilot channels will be configured, and who will maintain the shared prompt/config artifact after launch. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on the API contract freeze, the pilot setup, the handoff package, and ongoing ownership boundaries.

members.name: Nina Park
members.expertise: Internal developer tooling, workflow automation, Slack integrations, rollout coordination
members.background: Nina has spent five years building internal bots and CI/CD helpers for engineering organizations and now leads adoption work for tooling that changes team habits.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to launch on schedule with minimal rework from application teams, and she is trying to avoid taking long-term ownership for data schemas owned by another team.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says the interface is 'frozen', that means no breaking field-name or payload-shape changes for the pilot window, though additive metadata is still possible.
The 'pilot channels' are the three real squad channels where developers already work, with the bot posting read-only reminders alongside normal conversations.
A 'complete handoff' includes example payloads, expected edge cases, retry behavior notes, and the runbook link, because consuming teams need operational context as well as the schema.
The shared config lives in the existing GitOps repo managed by Developer Productivity, and platform-owned values are submitted there through pull requests.

members.name: Omar Haddad
members.expertise: Platform integrations, event pipelines, service ownership, operational reliability
members.background: Omar previously led messaging infrastructure at a larger enterprise and now manages the internal platform services that expose engineering activity into chat tools.
members.private_state: He wants to reduce operational ambiguity for his team, keep ownership lines clean, and avoid last-minute requests that expand the platform team's support surface during the pilot.
hidden_assumptions: When the interface is 'frozen', that means the versioned endpoint is stable, but individual fields can still be renamed before launch as long as the semantic contract is unchanged and the OpenAPI file is updated.
The 'pilot channels' are dedicated sandbox channels created for each squad so the bot can be tested without posting directly into live work channels.

A 'complete handoff' means the published OpenAPI spec, service account details, and a sample success response; operational behavior is already covered by standard platform conventions and need not be restated.

The shared config should live next to the event ingestion service in the platform repo until the pilot ends, because the emitting team should own message templates and routing defaults during early rollout.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the interface being frozen
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree that the API contract will be 'frozen by Friday'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina believes 'frozen' means no breaking payload changes at the field level for the duration of the pilot, so her team can wire the bot templates once and stop checking for schema churn.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Omar believes 'frozen' means the endpoint/version is fixed, but field names or nesting can still shift before launch if reflected in the official spec, because the contract is stable at the service version level.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are experienced engineers who routinely use 'contract freeze' as shorthand, so the phrase feels precise enough and neither expects the other to mean a materially different stability boundary.

misalignment_points.topic: Which channels are included in the pilot
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to setting up 'the three pilot channels'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina is thinking of the existing squad channels #payments-backend, #identity-api, and #search-infra where developers already coordinate daily work.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Omar is thinking of three new sandbox channels, one per squad, created specifically for pilot testing and isolated from live team discussions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have recently seen a list of the same three squad names and naturally assume that 'pilot channels' points to the same objects, even though one maps the names to existing channels and the other to new dedicated test channels.

misalignment_points.topic: What a complete Friday handoff contains
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say Omar's team will send a 'complete handoff package' on Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina expects completeness to include the schema, sample event payloads for normal and edge cases, retry semantics, and the runbook link so her team can safely configure messaging without additional back-and-forth.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Omar expects completeness to mean the formal spec, credentials, and one happy-path example, since anything else is optional documentation that can follow later if requested.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'complete handoff' sounds like routine coordination language, and each side assumes industry-standard packaging from the other's function without feeling the need to enumerate contents.

misalignment_points.topic: How the shared config will be maintained
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree that 'the shared config will live in one place' and that updates can go through PRs.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina assumes the one place is the existing Developer Productivity GitOps repo, where squads already manage bot rollout settings and where platform changes arrive as pull requests.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Omar assumes the one place is the Slack Platform service repo during the pilot, with downstream teams proposing changes there so the emitting service retains operational control.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both prefer Git-based change control and say 'single source of truth' and 'PR workflow', the high-level process sounds aligned even though the actual repository and owner differ.

turns.inner_thought: I want this meeting to lock down just enough so my team can finish wiring Handbot without getting dragged into owning platform-side schema churn or config stewardship that should sit elsewhere. If we can leave with Friday set for the handoff and the pilot plan firm for the three real squad channels, I can keep next week on track.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I wanted to use this to get Handbot lined up for next week's three-squad pilot and make sure we're aligned on Friday's handoff, the remaining integration details, and who owns what once we flip it on.

turns.inner_thought: Service is in decent shape. I can commit to the versioned endpoint and spec being settled by Friday, though I still want room to clean up field names if we catch anything awkward before launch. As long as they consume from the published spec, that should be a normal contract freeze.
turns.utterance: Yep, that all sounds right. From our side, the event ingestion service is stable, and we should have the API contract frozen by Friday.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. If frozen by Friday means no field-level breaking changes during the pilot, my team can finish the parser once, wire the reminder templates, and stop babysitting payload differences. Additive metadata is fine; I just don't want to revisit shape changes after we cut over.
turns.utterance: That works for us. Once the contract is frozen, we can wire the reminder templates and stop touching the parser before the pilot.

turns.inner_thought: Next thing is getting the three sandbox channels provisioned cleanly. I don't want this bot posting into live squad rooms until we've seen behavior in isolation. If access gets approved, my team can stand those up quickly.
turns.utterance: On rollout logistics, we can provision the three pilot channels as soon as service account access is approved.

turns.inner_thought: Good, because the leads for Payments, Identity, and Search already think Handbot is going into their existing team channels next week. I'll give them a heads-up about reminder volume so nobody is surprised when read-only posts start appearing alongside regular conversation.
turns.utterance: Great. The squad leads in Payments, Identity, and Search are already expecting posts in the pilot channels, and I'll warn them about message volume.

turns.inner_thought: I should set expectations on what my team is actually delivering Friday: the OpenAPI spec, service account details, and one sample success response. That is a complete handoff package from a platform standpoint. I don't want to implicitly sign us up for extra operational docs unless they ask later.
turns.utterance: For Friday, our complete handoff package will include the published spec, bot credentials, and a sample response so your team can finish the hookup quickly.

turns.inner_thought: Nice. If the complete handoff package includes the usual operational context too—examples, edge cases, retry notes, runbook—we can finalize channel rules and edge-case messaging without doing another round of Q&A. That should keep app teams from getting pulled into debugging during the pilot.
turns.utterance: Perfect. With the complete handoff, we should be able to finalize channel rules and edge-case messaging without blocking on follow-up questions.

turns.inner_thought: Now I need to keep the config under control. During the pilot, the cleanest line is to keep the shared config next to the platform service so my team can own routing defaults and templates that affect operational behavior. PRs are fine, but I don't want support ambiguity from files scattered across repos.
turns.utterance: The other thing I wanted to cover is the shared config. I think it should live in one place, and updates can go through PRs so the pilot stays controlled and auditable.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed. Keeping it in the existing Developer Productivity GitOps repo is the obvious move since squads already manage rollout YAML there, and platform-owned values can come in as pull requests. That avoids my team inheriting long-term schema ownership while still letting us coordinate rollout changes efficiently.
turns.utterance: Yeah, one place makes sense. Our team can update the rollout YAML there as squad preferences come in during the pilot.

turns.inner_thought: I should reinforce the boundary: platform monitors delivery and reliability; they handle wording and rollout coordination. As long as the config and service behavior stay under our repo during pilot, that split is clean and avoids late surprises landing on my on-call rotation.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. We'll monitor delivery health on our side, and Developer Productivity can handle message wording and squad coordination.

turns.inner_thought: So we're good: frozen by Friday means my team can stop worrying about payload churn, the complete handoff should let us finish integration, and early next week we can turn on the three live squad channels. If this holds, no one needs rework and I can keep the pilot on schedule.
turns.utterance: Okay, let me just play back what I heard: Friday we get the frozen contract and the complete handoff package, and then early next week we can light up the three pilot channels.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, that's the plan from my perspective. I'll send the docs and the PR path after this so they know where to pull from and propose changes. That should be enough to keep ownership clean and prevent any extra support surface from sneaking in before launch.
turns.utterance: That's the timeline. I'll send the docs and the PR path after the meeting so both teams can proceed.
